text: Hey Mike. Thanks. Thanks for that. Welcome. Just going to try and share my screen here. Hopefully we can get it to work. Are we good on everyone else's in there? I think that's a thumbs up. So we'll talk a little bit about commuter, about local and then, you know, some out there thoughts a little bit on kind of an integrated approach to connect to transit. So just a quick familiarization. So Pacific Western is a family-owned company headquartered in Calgary founded actually the family's out of the Tascoan area. Our founder, he actually started with GMAC and no one Tascoan Motors for many years and then got into school bus sales and kind of evolved from there. It's probably about 35 transit contracts throughout Canada and we actually have the contracts for all Alberta contracted services. So Cold Lakes in Albert, Port Saskatchewan, Dukes, Bruce Grove, Airdrie. We also have some vehicles with Access Calgary and it's I guess it's public knowledge, but we're the lead proponent for the City of Edmonton for their on-demand service that they're implementing as part of their bus network redesign. So the service in Edmonton will be the largest on-demand bus network in North America and we're just kind of in those contract negotiations with the city. So there will be more news on that for anyone that's not aware. And out of these transit contracts that we have, we have five that are demand-based transit systems. So some contracted on-demand. So again in Calgary, that's us, Cochrane. We've actually been doing an on-demand commuter transit link in Atchison now for about three and a half years and that just connects basically the commuter that runs between Spruce Grove and Edmonton into the Atchison Business Park and then basically moves commuters into their place of work. We're also working with Oak Tokes and Airdrie and then in Ontario and BC. We are not operating those but those are just examples of other contracted services in Canada that are demand-based. So we think about on-demand. I mean, Uber is probably the easiest comparison because I think most of us probably at one point or another have at least heard of Uber if not tried it. But you know, essentially it's an app and you can see the vehicle and you can order the vehicle and depending on the services you can order in advance. So we see in Cochrane, for instance, many of the users are commuters. So they use the on-demand service to connect into the commuter service that runs between Cochrane and Calgary. So they're booking their seat on the on-demand service a week in advance because they know that every morning they have to be at the commuter bus for 7 a.m. So they just book it. So that's kind of one spectrum of it. The other spectrum is really truly Uber-like demand, really demand-based. So City of Calgary, we're doing that. We see a lot of usage that is really truly real-time demand-driven. And in thinking about this, I mean, we really have to think about what the future holds in terms of mobility. It's really about personalization and it's again more so about mobility versus just transportations. How people move, how do they move safely, healthfully, things like walking and microtransit can all be part of this sort of bigger picture scheme of things. So as I mentioned, on-demand really has several components. So there's really an app for the driver. So driver gets basically information in real-time for pickups and drop-offs, etc. Then of course, the main side of it, there's the rider app and typically it's an iOS and Android and then web applications. In many circumstances, we also have call centers set up so people can call in and book over the phone. In some cases, we operate that. In other cases, the cities will handle those. But that's all part and parcel. Then there's an administration portal and that's where essentially all the levers are pulled, all the data set, all the parameters are set and that's set up where typically jointly between the municipality and ourselves, we have access so we can, again, in real-time either adjust or at least view data. The other piece is open API. So very easy to integrate. So when you talk about like Transit app or Google, things like that and then white labeling. All that is really developing it so where it's customized to the city. So it's rather than a PWT app, it becomes a City of Beaumont app and it's really easy to integrate other information and can be integrated the other way. So if Beaumont has some information on a portal, this can be pushed to that as well. So lots of flexibility. So the Rider app itself, again, if you've used Duper, it's very similar. So you download the app, you sign up, you put in your information and then you really have full access. Depending on the services in Cochrane, for instance, it's free. So there's no payment component, but if it's part of Transit and there wants to be, you guys would want to charge, that's easy to do and there's lots of flexibility in what that looks like as well. And then there's the driver component. So again, driver login and once the driver logs in, knows what vehicle the driver's in and that also pushes the information to the app. So the person waiting can see exactly which bus is going to pick them up and exactly where it's going to pick them up. And it gives the driver those details as well. Within the information within the app, both on the driver and passenger side, you can do cancellations, driver can track no-shows and all those kinds of things as well. And on the admin side of things, again, this is where all the system tools are. So it's design, it's just looking at basically all the data sets, all the parameters of what the system is in real time. So you don't need to wait till the end of the month to get a ridership report or anything like that. I mean, everything really is in real time. One interesting component is this last item, which is crowdsourcing. So what that really is. So when we set up an on-demand system, we work with the municipality and gather whatever data points there are. In many cases, we're using school bus data, for instance, as to where people are living and where they're moving, how they're moving, whether or not the municipality has any kind of existing transit, all these data sets. But what crowdsourcing really does is we can really start seeing almost immediately where people are searching. And so depending on the type of system you have, and you can do a door-to-door, you can do a curve-to-curve, a corner-to-corner. Most of the ones that we're doing are what we call congregated stops. So they're predetermined bus stops. So the app basically tells the prospective rider, okay, bus is going to pick you up in 12 minutes and you have to walk to this bus stop. And again, all those parameters could be set. What crowdsourcing does is that if, for instance, in an area, maybe there isn't a bus stop, but for whatever reason, there is high demand, maybe it's just a little bit of a hot zone for students, let's say, or maybe some workforce that are commuting that's maybe not as dense. So it's really easy to adjust and you can implement a prospective pickup spot there and kind of ease that. So there's a starting point, but the beauty of a system like this is that it's really fluid and flexible and can scale both up and down very, very easily. So we've got a little bit of information on the on-demand services that I mentioned. So City of Calgary, what we've been doing there, it's been operating for not quite a year, but it was in North Calgary and it's a newer development. So when we started, there were probably about a thousand or so, 1,200 people in the area and the service was really designed to feed into a big transit exchange 10-15 minutes away. So right away, initially, we started seeing that we're doing about 150 or so passengers a day and the biggest number that was quite promising is that there was about a 70% shared ride trend. So meaning that it's not that kind of Uber-style single passenger trips. They were all 70% were shared trips. So, and again, this is a community, no transit. It's new. So anyone moving in really, you know, they're prepared to drive. They knowingly moved in there, knowing that there wasn't any transit and we seen an immediate uptake. And for those that maybe have been following a little bit of the media, Calgary is really looking to expand this service. It's been really successful in this kind of initial piloted approach and we're working with them to grow it. So it's been great. And again, the other piece that's really a value here is this rider satisfaction rating. So to see a 4.8 out of 5 immediately is really telling. And again, this is another beautiful piece of going to a service like this is you get real-time live feedback as soon as the trip's done, you can basically be set up where the passenger just provides its simple star rating. So it could be 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and you get that easy feedback right away. The other service, as I mentioned, was Cochrane. So again, Cochrane had no transit at all in the community. Their services is accessible as well. So kind of killing two birds with one stone doing kind of the conventional passenger as well as the para passenger. Within the first three weeks, we were doing over 250 passengers a day. Some of it may have been contributed to the fact that it was free. But again, these services are typically, you know, a couple of dollars to similar to what transit would be. What Cochrane really found early on was that people were leaving their cars in their garage. So they were choosing to take the service rather than driving, parking in the park and ride and taking the commuter service. So that was really interesting. And again, real high percentage of shared rides and quite significant rider satisfaction rating as well. I should also maybe mention that with on-demand services, there's a number of models to work with. So for Cochrane, for instance, they own the vehicles and maintain them. We provide the service. We provide the drivers, the dispatch, the technology, the call center. In Calgary, we actually own the vehicles. So in Calgary, we started with two minivans, one being accessible and within two months, we had to grow to a 13-passenger sprinter style van. So we have that van and two minivans now operating in Calgary. So the models can be flexible. We can, a contractor like us, can certainly provide full-term key with vehicles and everything or the city can or it could be a potential mix. So looking at, you know, obviously Beaumont has the commuter service. So there's some opportunity in terms of looking at some options with it. So with the commuter, I mean, we sort of sought an opportunity and said, hey, you know, extending the route, kind of a bit more southbound through the community could really drive a little bit of ridership, you know, the buses and operations are really coming through. So how do you really leverage the existing service to really drive more ridership? So we believe there's, you know, a significant amount of opportunity to grow there with some, again, adjustment of routing and things like that. From a local perspective, I mean, we looked at it and, you know, we really don't think fixed route is the answer. Again, I think everything we've seen in communities where transit doesn't exist or didn't exist before, on-demand has been successful. And then just thinking about Beaumont's demographics, young families, I mean, I think tech savvy and with Beaumont being positioned as really a tech hub, I think there's a lot of alignment and I think there would be a lot of support. So on-demand, even aside from those factors, really makes sense in a community like Beaumont. Like I said, the beauty of it is that it's very easy to scale up and scale up and react really quickly and almost in real time. And then just looking at service hours, I mean, there's, I think, a lot of room and opportunity to kind of play around with, you know, extending certain peaks, potentially adding some midday in the commuter. And again, if we think about routing and service hours, it could really drive some ridership numbers. I think we're kind of getting to the end here. So, you know, the other piece we think about is really this connected approach and I think Beaumont's a well-positioned community to really leverage kind of three items that we think about is the commuter service. Again, lots of opportunity goes south, not just through the community, but thinking about the county in general, airport, the Duke, that kind of regional extension to the services and the connectivity that on-demand could really bring and feed into the commuter service as well. And again, I think there's lots of opportunity to cross-utilize equipment potentially in fleet. And again, the fleets there, it's already paid for. So how do we get better utilization? How do we grow ridership? And how do we sort of provide a service that people are going to want to use? And then the third component of that is the automated side of it. So again, you know, Beaumont was a test bed and there's a lot of opportunity to look at long-term potential integration with all three items into this greater connected mobility network, essentially, for the City of Beaumont. And that's it. Thank you, folks, for your time. If anyone has any questions, we'd happy to chat further.
